'''Alexander A. Beilinson''' (born 1957) is the David and Mary Winton Green University professor at the [[University of Chicago]] and works on mathematics.  His research  has spanned [[representation theory]], [[algebraic geometry]] and [[mathematical physics]].  In 1999, Beilinson was  awarded the [[Ostrowski Prize]] with [[Helmut Hofer]].
In 2017, he was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20170503160816/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/may-2-2017-NAS-Election.html National Academy of Sciences Members and Foreign Associates Elected], [[National Academy of Sciences]], May 2, 2017.</ref> In 2018, he received the [[Wolf Prize in Mathematics]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Paul McCartney among 9 Wolf Prize recipients |url=https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/culture/paul-mccartney-among-9-wolf-prize-recipients-542404 |access-date=May 21, 2020 |website=The Jerusalem Post &#124; JPost.com|date=12 February 2018 }}</ref> and in 2020 the [[Shaw Prize]] in Mathematics.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Shaw Prize |url=http://www.shawprize.org/prizes/mathematical-sciences |access-date=May 21, 2020 |website=www.shawprize.org}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Beilinson was born in Moscow of mostly [[Russians|Russian]] descent while his paternal grandfather was [[Jews|Jewish]]. Nevertheless he was discriminated against because of his Jewish surname, and was not admitted to [[Moscow State University]]. He went to the [[Moscow Pedagogical State University|Pedagogical Institute]] instead and transferred to Moscow State University when he was a third year student.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fuchs |first=Dmitry |title=On Soviet Mathematics of the 1950s and 1960s |url=http://math.uchicago.edu/~drinfeld/Golden%20years/Fuchs.pdf |pages=215–216}}</ref>

==Work==
In 1978, Beilinson published a paper on [[coherent sheaves]] and several problems in [[linear algebra]].  His two-page note in the journal ''Functional Analysis and Its Applications'' was one of the papers on the study of [[derived categories]] of coherent [[sheaf (mathematics)|sheaves]].

In 1981, Beilinson announced a proof of the [[Kazhdan–Lusztig conjectures]] and [[Jantzen conjectures]] with [[Joseph Bernstein]].  Independent of Beilinson and Bernstein, [[Jean-Luc Brylinski|Brylinski]] and [[Masaki Kashiwara|Kashiwara]] obtained a proof of the Kazhdan–Lusztig conjectures.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Brylinski|first1=Jean-Luc|last2=Kashiwara|first2=Masaki|title=Kazhdan-Lusztig conjecture and holonomic systems|date=October 1981|volume=64|journal=[[Inventiones Mathematicae]]|publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]]|pages=387–410|issn=0020-9910|doi=10.1007/BF01389272|issue=3|bibcode=1981InMat..64..387B|s2cid=18403883}}</ref>  However, the proof of Beilinson–Bernstein introduced a method of [[Localization of a category|localization]].  This established a geometric description of the entire [[category (mathematics)|category]] of representations of the [[Lie algebra]], by "spreading out" representations as geometric objects living on the [[flag variety]]. These geometric objects naturally have an [[intrinsic]] notion of [[parallel transport]]: they are [[D-modules]].

In 1982, Beilinson published his own conjectures about the existence of [[motivic cohomology]] groups for [[scheme (mathematics)|schemes]], provided as [[hypercohomology group]]s of a complex of [[abelian groups]] and related to [[algebraic K-theory]] by a [[motivic spectral sequence]], analogous to the [[Atiyah–Hirzebruch spectral sequence]] in [[algebraic topology]]. These conjectures have since been dubbed the [[Beilinson-Soulé conjectures]]; they are intertwined with [[Vladimir Voevodsky]]'s program to develop a [[homotopy theory]] for [[scheme (mathematics)|schemes]].

In 1984, Beilinson published the paper ''Higher Regulators and values of L-functions'', in which he related [[higher regulator]]s for K-theory and their relationship to [[L-functions]].  The paper also provided a generalization to [[arithmetic variety|arithmetic varieties]] of the [[Lichtenbaum conjecture]] for [[Algebraic K-theory|K-groups]] of number [[Ring (mathematics)|rings]], the [[Hodge conjecture]], the [[Tate conjecture]] about [[algebraic cycles]], the [[Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture]] about [[elliptic curves]], and [[Bloch's conjecture]] about ''K''<sub>2</sub> of elliptic curves.

Beilinson continued to work on [[algebraic K-theory]] throughout the mid-1980s.  He collaborated with [[Pierre Deligne]] on the developing a [[motive (algebraic geometry)|motivic]] interpretation of [[Don Zagier]]'s [[polylogarithm]] conjectures.

From the early 1990s onwards, Beilinson worked with [[Vladimir Drinfeld]] to rebuild the theory of [[vertex algebra]]s.  After some informal circulation, this research was published in 2004 in a form of a monograph on [[chiral algebra]]s. This has led to new advances in [[conformal field theory]], [[string theory]] and the geometric [[Langlands program]]. He was elected a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 2008.<ref name=AAAS>{{cite web|title=Book of Members, 1780–2010: Chapter B|url=http://www.amacad.org/publications/BookofMembers/ChapterB.pdf|publisher=American Academy of Arts and Sciences|access-date=May 30, 2011}}</ref> He was a visiting scholar at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in the fall of 1994 and again from 1996 to 1998.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.ias.edu/people/cos/frontpage?page=11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130106223448/http://www.ias.edu/people/cos/frontpage?page=11|url-status=dead|title=Institute for Advanced Study: A Community of Scholars|archive-date=January 6, 2013|access-date=May 21, 2020}}</ref>
